Yesterday I started to look at others’ PRs to see how far I am from being able to review. Definitely, I need some encouragement before continuing to catch up with the upstreams in Representation.Homological.ContCohomology.

Roughly, we already have the following things:

0) Resolution complex M → C(G, M) → ⋯ → C(G, C(G,...,C(G, M))) → ⋯

-1) Functoriality of 0) both in M and G

-2) A “wild” coeffiecnet category of topological representations TopRep k G (which is equivalent to Action (TopModule k) G). I put a “wild” here because the continuity on G is NOT assumed, i.e. making no use of the topology of G in this definition.

The main concern is about -2). Why do we choose “TopRep k G” as the ambient category and what is the benefit? It seems to me the only benefit of TopRep is that it provides the cheapest way to even state the resolution. I also assume that the chosen ambient category would provide some technical convenience for some particular future proofs. However, I see negative signs:

1) No adjoint functors have been introduced. In particular, no adjunction has been recorded for res coind in TopRep k G. In fact, the current res coind are simply NOT adjoint to each other. For example, if we take (1 : ⊥ →* G) then the adjunction would say
Hom_cont(V, W) ≅ Hom_TopRep(V, coind W) = Hom_TopRep(V, C(G, W))
This is NOT true: the intended image of f is v ↦ (g ↦ g f v), which may not be continuous because the continuity on G is NOT assumed.

2) The docstring of the current coind₁ claims that it is isomorphic to the continuous coinduction of the trivial representation of the trivial subgroup of G, i.e.
coind (1 : ⊥ →* G) trivial k G π.V ≅ coind₁ π
C(G, V) ≅ C(G, V)
where the LHS is right regular and the RHS sends g to the action f ↦ (x ↦ π g f (g⁻¹ * x)). This claim is FALSE for TopRep k G in general, because the intended intertwining map f ↦ (x ↦ π x f x⁻¹) may not send continuous functions to continuous ones, as the continuity on G is NOT assumed in our “wild” TopRep k G, and the current coind₁Equivcoind in Mathlib is NOT the same statement as in the above claim.

On the other hand, I think we actually want 1) and 2) to hold very much! Note that 1) and 2) do hold under stronger conditions, which suggests that 1) 2) are indeed close to desired form while they are just not true in TopRep.

Finally, the concern may be summarized as: If eventually we realize that we need a dream category have 0) 1) 2) at the same time (probably under suitable conditions on G or some other fine-tuned version of C(G, V)), then TopRep just adds an additional layer with no further payoff except for a plain definition. Does it really worth to add the abstract level TopRep now? Or TopRep does have some other technical advantages that I didn't realize (e.g. an alternative coind has been cooked up under this generality)?
I think representation is going through a big refactor right now (for example Action is going to disappear). Anyway the relevant person is @Edison Xie .

Well, the docstring is surely false and it needs to be fixed, thanks for pointing that out.

This part of the library is very new (and there a lot of moving pieces for reasons unrelated to representation theory, the new transparency settings, the monoid algebra refactor etc) so it's very possible that is not perfect. We are just trying to do our best.

I think that right now the development is very general. My guess is that one reason that there is no continuity hypothesis for the action is that in this generality there are two different continuity hypotheses that one could ask for (continuity of G x M -> M and continuity of G -> (M -> M)) and these do not coincide in general (topological spaces aren't a Cartesian closed category) and instead of saying "let's restrict to spaces where there is no ambiguity" we have said "let's just think about this problem later". This was my motivation behind my recent question in #maths asking in what generality people took cohomology of a topological group acting on a topological module.

I agree that TopRep is an abomination though, it's essentially never right and indeed it is merged now. To understand better what we should be doing we should first have a clearer picture of the generality in which we want to let topological groups act on topological abelian groups.

TopRep is just the categorical analogue of ContRepresentation, that contains a better explanation :"The reason for this more general definition is that it allows us to define the coinduced representation of a continuous representation as also a continuous representation without any restriction on the topology on G." I was convinced at the time that this was nice, but I probably didn't realize that also the second "continuous representation" in the sentence is in the weak sense and so this is much less interesting than it seems.

Kevin Buzzard said:

instead of saying "let's restrict to spaces where there is no ambiguity" we have said "let's just think about this problem later".

I am just worrying that if later on we need to change the coefficient category, say DreamContRep, we have to upgrade everything to DreamContRep. But then we would have to add compatibilities to TopRep for previous user whose work is based on TopRep, wouldn't that be considerable amount of maintainance (which should be avoidable if we just start from DreamContRep)? It seems to me like a trade-off between cheapest access to the defition and overall optimizaiton.

Also the word "coinduced representation" is not accurate, it is actually the "preresolution" functor 'coind_1' which supports the resolution complex and I believe this is the true "reason for this general definition"

Yes that one (I like the name preresolution, I wasn't happy with coind₁ but didn't find anything better). What about the following?

  • we refactor ContRepresentation to require the map G × V → V to be continuous
  • we require G to be locally compact, so the current C(G, V) design should still hold
I have no idea if someone cares about the continuous cohomology of nonlocally compact groups.
Not in this form, no. But people do care about infinite-dimensional Lie groups and their cohomology, and the relation to Lie algebra cohomology for inf. dim. Lie algebras

Right -- this was the discussion I was trying to have in #maths > Continuous cohomology . In what generality do people care about cohomology where there is some continuity condition on the cocycles? I feel we're still not at the bottom of this and my instinct is that it should inform our design decisions unless there is some more general theory which mathematicians haven't isolated but which is natural in our context. I worry that TopRep is none of those things.
I will point out that Banach- and Fréchet-Lie groups are of interest, so things like local compactness are hit-and-miss

Let me stress that anyway the current definition of continuous cohomology is mathematically correct (i.e. coincides with the usual one) is G is locally compact and the map G × V → V is continuous.
What it seems to be a problem is that the second assumption is complicated to state in practice in TopRep, since you need another category, but it's easy in ContRepresentation (it's just another typeclass). On the other hand being G locally compact is not a problem, we can just assume it wherever it's needed.

I don't think the issue is the mathematical correctness of the cohomology. For whatever your DreamContRep is, as long as underlying the resolution complex is unchanged, it will provide the correct cohomology groups for practical use. The point is what technical advantage DreamContRep buys you? I don't see promising answer for TopRep

It's just more general. This was the initial point, if something can be stated in bigger generality we often do so, even if we don't have a concrete example. What you are pointing out is a drawback of the current approach, that certain results only hold with an additional assumption and this is complicated to state.
What may be the solution is to change TopRep to assume continuity of G × V → V, since almost surely nobody will complain, but not assuming locally compactness. This is easy to state when needed.

Probably this is the minimum to do, at least trackable from literature.

What is done in the literature is only partially relevant. The authors of continuous cohomology know the standard approach of course, and not following it is a deliberate decision. Of course we want to get the same results in the usual cases (and this is OK) while keeping things usable. It's this last part that is maybe less clear, but if we just assume everything that is assumed in all the standard references then we pay a very high price when someone says "I am not assuming X but everything I am using works without it". This happens quite frequently in the literature, so it's better to be prepared.

Well, it would be fine to ask for generality if it is mathematically clear. However, since there seems to be no satisfactory naive topological cohomology theory (look at what condensed Mathematics complains), it would be challenging to keep generality on this part. I do appreciate the current approach as a nice try.
Can compactly-generated replace locally compact, at least in on-paper mathematics? How is the local compactness even being used?
Asking a very naive Q I know
It's used to get the isomorphism C(G,C(G,V)) ≃ₜ C(G × G, V) via Homeomorph.curry.
And it's not even currently used, but it's one of the reasons why the definition agrees with the standard one.

Hi all I’m glad to see so many people care about cohomology theory in Mathlib! However I won’t be able to reply for at least quite a while -my connection is bad on plane and we’re kinda going through a thunderstorm :thunderstorm:

TopRep just uses the condition that for each element of G, the linear map V \to V is continuous. There are obviously much stronger continuity conditions that we could impose. However, if we do that then (unless G is locally compact) the resolution will not be in the same category. For example if we assume that G x V \to V is continuous, it does not follow that G x C(G,V) \to C(G,V) is continuous unless G is locally compact.

For exactly the same reason, if N is a normal subgroup of G then there's no reason why (G/N) x H^r(N,V) \to H^r(N,V) should be continuous. Hence, in order to define H^r(G/N, H^s(N,V)) when G is not locally compact, we need more generality than just assuming G x V \to V is continuous.
